work: 1/lambda = R_H(1/4 - 1/16) = 1.097e7 x 0.1875 = 2.057e6 m^-1. lambda = 1/2.057e6 = 4.86e-7 m = 486 nm. This matches the blue-green H-beta line of the Balmer series.
cleanExplanation: Use 1/lambda = R_H(1/n_low^2 - 1/n_high^2) = 1.097e7 (1/2^2 - 1/4^2) = 1.097e7 x 0.1875 = 2.057e6 m^-1. Inverting gives lambda = 4.86e-7 m, or 486 nm. This is the blue-green H-beta line of the Balmer series.

work: The rule is l <= n - 1. For n = 2 only l = 0 or 1 are allowed, so l = 2 is impossible; also m_l = 1 is not permitted for l = 2 when n = 2. The other sets satisfy l < n and |m_l| <= l.
cleanExplanation: An orbital set is valid only if l is at most n - 1 and |m_l| is at most l. For n = 2 the allowed l values are 0 and 1, so the set (2, 2, 1, -1/2) is unacceptable. All other listed sets obey the quantum-number restrictions.

work: E = h x nu = 6.626e-34 J s x 5.45e14 s^-1 = 3.61e-19 J. This is physically reasonable for one visible photon (a few eV).
cleanExplanation: For a single photon, E = h nu = (6.626e-34 J s)(5.45e14 s^-1) = 3.61e-19 J. That is about 2.3 eV, as expected for a green photon.

work: Heisenberg: delta_p >= h/(4 pi delta_x) = 6.626e-34/(4 x 3.1416 x 1.0e-10) = 5.27e-25 kg m/s. Choice B (1.05e-24) corresponds to using delta_p delta_x >= h/2 with h instead of h-bar, i.e., a factor-of-2 error.
cleanExplanation: The minimum uncertainty follows from delta_p delta_x >= h/(4 pi). Thus delta_p >= 6.626e-34 J s / (4 x 3.1416 x 1.0e-10 m) = 5.27e-25 kg m/s.

work: Cr (Z = 24) has the anomalous configuration [Ar]4s^1 3d^5: one electron in 4s plus five singly occupied 3d orbitals, giving 6 unpaired electrons. The [Ar]4s^2 3d^4 option would give 4 unpaired and is not the ground state.
cleanExplanation: Chromium's ground state is [Ar]4s^1 3d^5 because half-filling both the 4s and 3d subshells lowers electron-electron repulsion. With five singly occupied 3d orbitals plus the single 4s electron, there are 6 unpaired electrons.

work: Total nodes = n - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 for any 4s orbital. Since l = 0, all three are radial nodes (angular nodes = l = 0).
cleanExplanation: The total number of nodes of an orbital equals n - 1, so a 4s orbital has 3 total nodes. Because l = 0, the number of angular nodes is zero, so all 3 nodes are radial.

work: Wavelength increases with decreasing frequency/energy: gamma < X-ray < UV < visible < IR < microwave < radio. Only choice A orders them gamma < UV < IR < radio.
cleanExplanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths and radio waves the longest. So the order of increasing wavelength is gamma rays < ultraviolet < infrared < radio waves.

work: Transitions ending at n = 1 are the Lyman series (all wavelengths in the far UV). Balmer ends at n = 2, Paschen at n = 3, and Brackett at n = 4.
cleanExplanation: Spectral series are named for the lower level of the transition. Transitions to n = 1 form the Lyman series, which lies in the ultraviolet; the Balmer, Paschen and Brackett series end at n = 2, 3 and 4 respectively.

work: Cu (Z = 29) is [Ar]4s^1 3d^10, an anomalous configuration (the 4s electron shifts into 3d to complete the d subshell). Ti is [Ar]4s^2 3d^2, Zn is [Ar]4s^2 3d^10 (already filled/regular), and Fe is [Ar]4s^2 3d^6, all regular by Aufbau.
cleanExplanation: Among these elements only copper deviates from the Aufbau filling order, having [Ar]4s^1 3d^10 rather than [Ar]4s^2 3d^9. Titanium, zinc and iron all follow the regular filling pattern. Copper's anomaly reflects the extra stability of a completely filled 3d subshell.

work: Born interpretation: |psi|^2 is a probability density, so |psi|^2 dV gives the probability of finding the electron in volume element dV. Energy, spin and velocity are not obtained from |psi|^2.
cleanExplanation: By the Born interpretation, |psi|^2 is the probability density for the electron at a point in space, so |psi|^2 dV is the probability of finding the electron in a small volume dV. It says nothing directly about energy, spin or velocity.
KHP reacts with NaOH in a 1:1 mole ratio. Moles KHP = 0.5105 g / 204.22 g/mol = 2.500e-3 mol, so 2.500e-3 mol NaOH is used. Dividing by 0.02420 L gives [NaOH] = 0.1033 M.

work: Some titrant delivered from the buret only fills the space left by the dislodged bubble instead of reaching the flask. The buret reading change is therefore larger than the true volume delivered, so calculated moles of titrant, and hence the reported analyte concentration, come out too high.
cleanExplanation: When the bubble escapes, part of the titrant recorded on the buret fills the tip and never reaches the flask. The recorded volume is thus larger than the volume actually delivered, so the analyte concentration calculated from it is reported higher than the true value.

work: Standard practice after a water rinse is to rinse with several small portions of the titrant so residual water does not dilute the delivered solution. Burets are not dried with paper, ovens or ethanol.
cleanExplanation: After rinsing with distilled water, the buret is rinsed two to three times with small portions of the titrant. This removes residual water so the titrant concentration in the buret is not diluted by water left on the walls.

work: Digestion (aging the precipitate in warm mother liquor) dissolves tiny particles and reprecipitates them onto larger crystals via Ostwald ripening. Large crystals are easier to filter, occlude less impurity, and resist peptization during washing.
cleanExplanation: Digestion keeps the precipitate in contact with the warm mother liquor so small, easily lost crystals dissolve and regrow onto larger crystals (Ostwald ripening). The resulting coarse crystals filter faster, hold fewer adsorbed impurities, and can be washed without peptizing.

work: Quantitative gravimetry requires a filter that retains fine BaSO4 crystals and leaves negligible residue on ignition. Ashless fine-porosity quantitative paper meets both needs; qualitative paper leaves appreciable ash and the coarse grade passes fines.
cleanExplanation: BaSO4 is a fine precipitate that must be collected quantitatively and then ignited in a crucible. Ashless, fine-porosity quantitative filter paper catches the fine crystals and burns away with negligible residue, so no weighed filter ash contaminates the result.

work: MnO4^- is intensely purple and its reduction product Mn2+ is nearly colorless, so the first persistent faint pink tint signals a slight excess of titrant. This self-indicating behavior removes the need for an added indicator.
cleanExplanation: Permanganate ion is deeply purple while the Mn2+ produced in acid is essentially colorless. The endpoint is signalled by the first lasting faint pink color from excess MnO4^-, so the titrant serves as its own indicator.

work: Starch forms an intense blue-black complex with triiodide; if added while much I3^- is present the complex forms in bulk and releases iodine slowly, causing a late, erratic endpoint. Starch is therefore added only when the yellow iodine color has faded to pale straw.
cleanExplanation: Starch binds strongly to triiodide, and adding it while large amounts of iodine remain makes the iodine slow to be released near the endpoint. So starch is added only when the yellow color has faded to pale straw, giving a sharp blue-to-colorless endpoint.

Moles of precipitate = 0.4820 g / 288.91 g/mol = 1.668e-3 mol, and each formula unit contains one Ni atom, so mass of Ni = 1.668e-3 mol x 58.69 g/mol = 0.0979 g. Dividing by the 0.6240 g sample gives a mass fraction of 0.157, or 15.7%.

work: A two- or three-point calibration with buffers spanning the pH range of interest corrects both slope and offset responses. Single-point calibration at an irrelevant temperature, acetone rinses, and wiping the bulb dry all damage accuracy.
cleanExplanation: Proper pH-meter practice is a two- or three-point calibration using fresh standard buffers that bracket the pH values to be measured. This corrects both the electrode slope and the offset over the working range; single-point calibration, acetone rinsing, and dry wiping the glass bulb all introduce error.
